documentation.title: Depot CI compatibility with GitHub Actions
documentation.description: Reference for GitHub Actions syntax, triggers, and configuration that Depot CI supports, including current limitations.
headings: Depot CI compatibility with GitHub Actions (https://depot.dev/docs/ci/compatibility)
Pull request workflows triggered from forks [#pull-request-workflows-triggered-from-forks]
documentation.applicability: Expanded workflow execution, orchestration, current-source checks, tests and debugging
documentation.reviewState: Complete deployed page, claims, repository applicability and actual receipt boundaries reviewed by parent

findings: The compatibility table marks workflow DAGs, matrices, reusable workflows, concurrency, outputs, services, containers, expressions and continuation supported; exercised continuation/timeout/rerun semantics retain their actual mismatches rather than inheriting the table's checkmarks.

Deployment environments are marked unsupported in the compatibility table; the separate secrets guide still supports environment-name metadata for variant matching. Metadata selection must not be confused with protected approval gates. Non-Depot runs-on labels become Linux depot-ubuntu-latest, so copied Windows/Mac labels cannot qualify operating-system execution.
Fork pull_request and pull_request_target support is documented as planned. Defensive fork behavior in individual Actions is a distinct layer, not proof of native fork workflow support.

Native scheduled workflows activate only on the default branch, use UTC, ignore per-entry timezone and have no start-time SLA. Repository dispatch also uses the default branch; workflow_run exposes distinct YAML name, path and Depot basepath fields.

Cross-repository reusable workflows require full commit SHAs or version-looking tags, not branches/abbreviated SHAs; authored .github/workflows paths resolve to .depot/workflows in the source repository. Private callers/source repositories have same-organization/App-access restrictions.
Unsupported permission keys are silently ignored. code-quality must be explicit and is excluded from read-all/write-all; issues permissions also depend on the Code Access App installation grant.
JavaScript Action Node12/16/20 declarations now run on Node24 by default, separately from the PATH node used by run steps; the temporary insecure-version opt-out is not a Node26 job-runtime fix.

GitHub Packages authentication with native GitHub App GITHUB_TOKEN is documented unsupported across package registries. Depot Registry save avoids introducing a broad long-lived package PAT; no PAT is provisioned in this research.
sourceReview.use: Keep GitHub orchestration for platform/environment/trust boundaries it supplies; design native owner jobs with explicit supported labels, permissions, immutable reusable references and separately qualified status/process/artifact behavior.
sourceReview.limits: Documentation is not actual exercise of every trigger, expression, reusable-workflow mode, fork trust boundary or permission. No recurring schedule, deployment environment, App installation or token is changed. Existing execution receipts qualify only their exact exercised boundaries.

depot/cache-mount creates and reuses a durable named filesystem, supports simultaneous mounts and conditional writes, but supplies no atomicity for overlapping application writes. Single writers, partitioned directories or immutable content-addressed entries remain application responsibilities.

sourceReview.limits: No organization retention/settings/listing is accessed. The existing single-pair timing does not establish a cache or whole-job speed multiplier, simultaneous-writer safety, or future beta pricing.

findings: Local ci run patches are injected after checkout; remote branches use unpushed changes and local-only branches use the default branch base. Reusable-workflow call jobs cannot receive a patch step and instead run merge-base code with a warning, so clean pushed immutable source avoids that local-patch coverage gap.

ci dispatch accepts a workflow basename and validates declared inputs; it differs from local ci run's workflow path/patch semantics. Depot actor identity derives from the actual dispatch credential and triggering_actor changes on retries while original actor remains fixed.

The built-in DEPOT_TOKEN is limited to the current job attempt and cannot dispatch another workflow; native job OIDC cannot directly authorize ci dispatch either. The guide's cross-workflow example requires a separately stored organization/user token, which is not introduced here.

Workflow --failed retry creates attempts for failed/cancelled jobs and also reruns downstream succeeded/skipped jobs. Single-job retry, in-step retry, full workflow rerun and a fresh dispatch have distinct replay scopes and costs.

Rerun requires a terminal workflow. Cancel can target run/workflow/job, but observed terminal state does not prove descendant absence or VM billing release; existing timeout and stale-artifact controls remain authoritative for those narrower boundaries.

Run/job/workflow show APIs expose exact hierarchy and attempts. Existing exact-owned status/watch/API/ZIP receipts avoid reading an organization-wide run list and join current immutable content rather than trusting numeric artifact ID order.

sourceReview.limits: No broad dispatch token, organization listing, production trigger or recurring workflow is configured. findings: Native parallel blocks fork step-state snapshots of outputs/environment/GITHUB_PATH, then merge state before the next step, while workspace, HOME and tool caches remain shared.
Secret masking takes effect globally and immediately across sibling branches; state isolation does not imply filesystem isolation.
A parallel block can contain ordered sequential arrays. Nested parallel blocks are unsupported, and step IDs must be unique across the entire job.

Default fail-fast cancels siblings; fail-fast:false lets failures complete without converting the group to success. Individual step continue-on-error absorbs its failure into group eligibility, distinct from documented job-level continuation and the measured native aggregate mismatch.

Shared Node builds must finish before module/browser fanout, and Cargo/other writers need distinct output ownership. The current coherent graph implements its own bounded process DAG inside a shell, so that new timing alone is not evidence for every native parallel-step state rule.
sourceReview.use: Use native parallel/sequential only for disjoint filesystem writers after prerequisites, with explicit failure collection and unique IDs; retain the prior source-bound orchestration receipts for the actual semantics exercised.
sourceReview.limits: The guide gives no conflict-precedence guarantee for sibling writes to the same state key or filesystem path. No new claim about signal propagation, billing release or nested parallel support follows.

documentation.title: Retry failed steps
documentation.description: Use the native retry key to automatically re-run a failed run step in Depot CI, with configurable backoff between attempts.
documentation.applicability: Expanded workflow execution, orchestration, current-source checks, tests and debugging
documentation.reviewState: Complete deployed page, claims, repository applicability and actual receipt boundaries reviewed by parent

findings: Native retry is supported only on run steps; retry on uses Actions is rejected because action post/state machinery is not safely replayable. A countN means N additional attempts, with1to10 retries and configurable constant/exponential capped delays.

Any nonzero failure triggers retry, without exit/output filters. continue-on-error applies only after all retries are exhausted; timeout-minutes is per attempt, while the job's cancellation/timeout stops further retries according to the guide.
Retries reuse the same sandbox. Filesystem mutations and GITHUB_OUTPUT/GITHUB_ENV/GITHUB_PATH/GITHUB_STATE contents accumulate; the files are read once after the loop and the last value wins.
All step-attempt groups share the same step logs rather than separate job-attempt logs, so attempt costs and failure evidence must distinguish step repeats from ci rerun jobs/workflows.

Repeated frozen-source assertions should remain evidence, not be hidden by unconditional retries. Current coherent graph samples intentionally use no retry; the measured finite-writer timeout gap also prevents inferring descendant process cleanup from retry/cancellation documentation.
sourceReview.use: Consider finite retries only for specifically identified transient, replay-safe commands, with admitted output identities and a job-level cost/time bound; preserve every failure and distinguish same-sandbox state from fresh reruns.
sourceReview.limits: No general retry policy is enabled. The guide's cancellation claim is not observed process absence, deallocation or billing release; native timeout controls retain their measured mismatch.

contextIndex.title: Can I run GitHub Actions workflows locally before pushing?
contextIndex.description: Yes. Depot CI can run a GitHub Actions workflow against your local working tree on remote CI compute. act can also simulate many Linux workflows locally in Docker.

contextIndex.title: Can I SSH into a CI runner to debug a failed build?
contextIndex.description: Yes, as long as the CI runner is still running. With Depot CI, you can attach to a live job or rerun it with an SSH session paused at the exact step you need to inspect.

contextIndex.title: How to use Depot as an alternative to GitHub
contextIndex.description: Host your Git repositories with Depot Code and run your GitHub Actions workflows on Depot CI. Set up a standalone repository or a GitHub mirror, push your code, and run tests from Depot.

contextIndex.title: How can I benchmark build execution speed across CI platforms?
contextIndex.description: Run the same commit and commands side by side on equivalent runners, then compare queue time, startup time, cache performance, execution time, reliability, and cost per completed job.

contextIndex.title: How can I build AMD64 and ARM64 Docker images in GitHub Actions?
contextIndex.description: Use Depot to build AMD64 and ARM64 images on native x86 and Arm machines in parallel, then push both variants under one multi-platform image tag. Local and CI builds can share the same persistent layer cache.

contextIndex.title: How can I debug flaky tests and intermittent CI failures?
contextIndex.description: Use Depot test analytics to find tests that pass and fail on the same commit, inspect the exact attempt, reproduce it in the runner, and rerun only the failed job. Retries should confirm a flake, not hide one.

contextIndex.title: How can I eliminate GitHub Actions queue times?
contextIndex.description: Switch jobs to GitHub Actions runners managed by Depot to remove queue times caused by runner capacity. Depot has no concurrency limits and provisions a fresh, single-tenant runner for every job.

contextIndex.title: How can I monitor GitHub Actions performance and cost across my organization?
contextIndex.description: Monitor GitHub Actions runners managed by Depot across your organization, find slow and failing jobs, inspect resource usage, right-size runners, search logs, and connect runtime to cost.

contextIndex.title: How can I reduce GitHub Actions costs without rewriting my workflows?
contextIndex.description: Reduce GitHub Actions costs with Depot runners and remote caching, then cut obsolete runs and unnecessary storage. Measure the jobs driving your bill and keep your existing workflow YAML, actions, and test commands.

contextIndex.title: How can I run Node.js tests in parallel in CI?
contextIndex.description: Use Depot CI to split Node.js tests across parallel matrix jobs and balance each shard with historical JUnit timings. For smaller workflows, parallel steps can also overlap tests with linting and type checks inside one job.

contextIndex.title: How can I share a Docker layer cache across GitHub Actions jobs?
contextIndex.description: Send every Docker build to the same Depot project. Depot automatically persists the BuildKit layer cache on remote NVMe storage so GitHub Actions jobs, workflow runs, and teammates can reuse it without uploading cache archives.

contextIndex.title: How can I speed up Docker builds in GitHub Actions?
contextIndex.description: Run Docker builds on Depot’s remote BuildKit builders with a persistent NVMe layer cache. You can keep GitHub Actions and migrate from docker/build-push-action with a small workflow change.

contextIndex.title: How can I speed up Node.js builds in GitHub Actions?
contextIndex.description: Run the workflow on faster GitHub Actions runners managed by Depot, cache package manager downloads, reuse build output, and parallelize independent tests. Most Node.js workflows can start with a one-line runner change.

contextIndex.title: How do ephemeral GitHub Actions runners work?
contextIndex.description: An ephemeral GitHub Actions runner is a fresh machine assigned to one job and destroyed when that job finishes. Each job starts clean, while caches and artifacts persist in external storage.

contextIndex.title: How do I build a container image once and promote it across environments?
contextIndex.description: Build and test the image once with Depot, save it to Depot Registry, capture its immutable digest, and deploy that same digest to staging and production. Promotion should change the release pointer, not rebuild the image.

contextIndex.title: How do I migrate from self-hosted GitHub Actions runners without rewriting workflows?
contextIndex.description: Move from self-hosted GitHub Actions runners to Depot by changing the runs-on label. Your workflow steps, actions, secrets, checks, and GitHub interface stay the same while Depot operates the runner fleet.

contextIndex.title: How do I share secrets and configuration across CI pipelines?
contextIndex.description: Define each secret or variable once in Depot CI, then use scoped variants for repositories, branches, workflows, and environments. The workflow keeps one stable name while Depot selects the most specific matching value.

contextIndex.title: How do I test AI-generated pull requests in CI?
contextIndex.description: Run the same required checks for AI-generated pull requests as human changes, but let the agent validate locally first, scope reruns to the failing job, and keep secrets and deployment permissions behind explicit trust boundaries.

contextIndex.title: How to build iOS and Android apps without managing CI runners
contextIndex.description: Run iOS builds on Depot macOS runners, Android builds on Linux, and accelerated Android Emulator tests in Depot CI. Keep your build tools without maintaining a runner fleet.

contextIndex.title: Should I self-host GitHub Actions runners?
contextIndex.description: Usually not. Self-host GitHub Actions runners only when you need hardware, policy, or runtime control that a managed runner can't provide. For speed, cost, or private network access, Depot is usually the simpler answer.

contextIndex.title: What are the best alternatives to GitHub-hosted Actions runners?
contextIndex.description: Depot is the best alternative to GitHub-hosted Actions runners for most teams. It keeps existing GitHub Actions workflows intact while providing faster, ephemeral runners for Linux, Windows, and macOS.

contextIndex.title: What is Depot?
contextIndex.description: Depot is a software delivery platform that accelerates container builds, GitHub Actions, CI workflows, and build caching.

contextIndex.title: What is the best remote cache for a large polyglot monorepo?
contextIndex.description: Depot Cache is the best remote cache for most large polyglot monorepos. It gives Bazel, Go, Gradle, Maven, Pants, sccache, and Turborepo one remote service for sharing valid build outputs across developers and CI.

contextIndex.title: What is the best way to cache large TypeScript monorepo builds?
contextIndex.description: Use a task graph to build only affected packages, content hashes to identify reusable work, and Depot Cache to share those outputs across developer machines and CI. Turborepo with Depot Cache is the best default for most TypeScript monorepos.

contextIndex.title: What is the fastest way to set up CI for a monorepo with many services?
contextIndex.description: Migrate the existing GitHub Actions workflow to Depot CI, model each service as an independent matrix job, and use a shared remote cache or custom CI image so 15 services can validate concurrently without reinstalling the world.

contextIndex.title: Why are my GitHub Actions builds slow?
contextIndex.description: GitHub Actions is usually slow because jobs wait for runners, rebuild dependencies, run sequential work, miss caches, or spend too long uploading artifacts. Measure each phase before changing the workflow.

methods.description: Cancels a queued, waiting, or running job and its active attempt.
Cancels a queued or running CI run and any of its unfinished workflows, jobs, and attempts.

methods.summary: Exports a finite snapshot of persisted log lines.
methods.description: The response is a Connect/gRPC server stream, not a raw HTTP file download. Consume it with a generated client or a decoder that understands stream framing. Read the first metadata response, then append each following chunk response to a file or writer in order. Use the Depot CLI `depot ci logs --output-file` when a shell-native file download is needed.
Returns a short-lived signed HTTPS URL for one artifact. The URL expires 5 minutes after issuance.
Returns an attempt's identity, status, timestamps, and sandbox/session IDs, with parent run, workflow, and job context.

methods.summary: Returns a failure diagnosis for a run, workflow, job, or attempt.
methods.description: For run and workflow targets, identical failures are grouped together by error fingerprint. For job and attempt targets, the response is a focused diagnosis of that single job or attempt. When too many jobs failed to diagnose individually, the response is a per-workflow and per-job breakdown instead. When no failure evidence is found, the response is empty. The response is limited to a fixed size and reflects the run's current state. The diagnosis can change while a run is in progress. As more jobs fail, a later call can surface new failures or turn an empty result into a grouped one. As job summaries become available, a later call can also add summary drill-down commands.
Returns a job's identity, status, timestamps, runner configuration, parent run and workflow context, dependencies, and attempt history.

Returns persisted log lines for a job attempt, oldest first. Identify the attempt by `attemptId`, or by `jobId` to use the job's latest attempt. Poll with `pageToken` to fetch lines persisted after a previous response.
Returns CPU and memory metrics for one job attempt.
Returns per-attempt CPU and memory metric summaries for one job.
Returns authored step summary markdown for a job, a specific attempt, or both.
Returns a CI run's identity, repo, trigger, status, and timestamps. For nested workflow, job, and attempt status, use `GetRunStatus`.
Returns workflow, job, and attempt CPU and memory metric summaries for one run.
Returns a CI run's status with its nested workflows, jobs, and attempts. For the run's identity, repo, trigger, and timestamps, use `GetRun`.
Returns a workflow's identity, status, timestamps, parent run context, execution history, and nested jobs and attempts.
Returns CI artifact metadata for one run, optionally narrowed to a workflow, job, or attempt. Download URLs are not included; request one per artifact with `GetArtifactDownloadURL`.

Returns CI runs for the authenticated organization, newest first. Filter by status, repository, commit SHA, trigger, or pull request number. Use `pageSize` and `pageToken` to page through additional results.
Returns CI workflows for the authenticated organization, newest first. Filter by name, repository, status, trigger, commit SHA, or pull request number. Use `pageSize` to return up to 200 workflows.
Resets every job in a workflow that's in a terminal state (finished, failed, or cancelled) to queued and runs them all again. Cancel the workflow first if it's still running.

Retries the failed and cancelled jobs in a workflow, along with every job that depends on them. A dependent that already succeeded or was skipped runs again too, because a job it consumed is running again. Queued dependents are left untouched, since they re-check their dependencies before starting. Fails without resetting anything when a waiting or running job depends on the retried set; wait for that job to finish, or cancel the workflow and use `RerunWorkflow`.
Retries a failed or cancelled job, along with any skipped jobs that depend on it. Fails when a job that depends on it has already started; use `RetryFailedJobs` to retry related failures together.
Triggers a CI run. Runs can contain one or more workflows.

methods.summary: Follows a job attempt's persisted log lines, streaming new lines while the attempt runs.
methods.description:
The response is a Connect/gRPC server stream, not raw text. Consume it with a generated client or a decoder that understands stream framing. Every response reports the attempt's current status. Responses that carry a log line also include `nextCursor`.

 To resume a dropped stream, save the newest `nextCursor` and send it as `cursor` on a new request. The new stream picks up after the last line you received. The stream ends on its own once the attempt has finished, failed, or been cancelled and all persisted lines have been sent.

faq.question: Which plan is right for me?
faq.answer:
The Developer plan is perfect for solo developers, side-projects, and experiments. It includes 500 Docker build minutes, 2,000 GitHub Actions minutes, 2,000 Depot CI minutes, and 1 user, with additional usage billed monthly.
The Startup plan is great for teams building production applications. It includes 5,000 Docker build minutes, 20,000 GitHub Actions minutes, 20,000 Depot CI minutes, and unlimited users, with additional usage billed monthly.
The Business plan is for dev teams looking to scale, and includes additional security controls and deployment models.

faq.question: What is Depot Cloud?
faq.answer: Depot Cloud is fully managed remote build infrastructure, including both compute and cache. With Depot Cloud, we handle the infrastructure and orchestration, with no need to manage your own build infrastructure. Depot Cloud runs on AWS, and is available in the us-east-1 and eu-central-1 regions.

faq.question: What is the usage granularity?
faq.answer: Docker build minutes and GitHub Actions minutes are billed on a per-minute basis, tracked per second. Depot CI usage is billed per second based on vCPU-seconds. We don't enforce a one-minute minimum, so if you run a 30-second Docker or GitHub Actions build, you'll only be billed for 30 seconds. Test results are billed per individual passing test.

faq.question: Can I self-host Depot? What is bring-your-own-compute?
faq.answer:
You can connect an AWS account to your Depot account and Depot will use that account for build compute and cache storage. This ensures that your build data is entirely under your control and allows you to access any private services in your account during the build. Additionally you can customize the types of machines used for your builds.

Bring your own compute is available on the Business plan.

Read more in our Depot Managed documentation

faq.question: Am I charged for build usage and storage?
faq.answer:
You are charged monthly for build usage and storage. See usage granularity above for how build time is measured.

Storage is a single combined total that covers your container build cache, Depot Cache, and Depot Registry. All three draw from your plan's included storage, and anything above that amount is billed at $0.20 per GB per month. Storage is billed as the average storage used over the month, sampled hourly.

Data transfer into and out of Depot Registry is free on the default Standard CDN speed. If you switch your organization to Fast CDN speed, data served out of the registry is billed at $0.10 per GB, from the first GB. Read more in our registry documentation.

faq.question: When will I be billed?
faq.answer: Depot bills monthly on the 1st. If you sign up partway through a month, your first charge is prorated for the remaining days. Usage-based charges accrue through the month and appear on your next invoice on the 1st along with your plan charge for that month.

faq.question: How are test results billed?
faq.answer:
The Developer and Startup plans each include 1,000,000 passing test results per month at no charge. After that, it's $0.000001 per passing test, or $1 per 1 million tests. Failed, errored, and skipped tests are free.

Read more in our test results documentation

faq.question: Are there discounts for non-profits or open-source?
faq.answer: Yes! Please contact us with more information about your project and for more details.

faq.question: Do you offer credits for startups?
faq.answer:
Yes, through our startup partner programs. Y Combinator companies can claim Depot credits from the YC deals page.

Startups approved for PostHog for Startups receive a partner code worth $5,000 in Depot credits. See our PostHog for Startups documentation for how to redeem it and what it covers.

faq.question: Can I cap my usage so my bill doesn't run over?
faq.answer: Yes, you can set self-imposed usage caps to control monthly usage. If you reach a cap, Depot will stop running builds until the next month or until you raise the cap. You can change these limits at any time.

faq.question: What payment methods are accepted?
faq.answer: For the Developer and Startup plans, we support monthly payments via credit card using Stripe. For the Business plan, we additionally support invoice billing, ACH, and AWS Marketplace.

faq.question: Can I pay through the AWS Marketplace?
faq.answer: Yes! We support AWS Marketplace billing on the Business plan. Contact us for more details.

draftParagraphs.text: Allocate these as complementary products: GitHub remains the authoritative forge and check consumer; retain its workflow orchestration where release permissions or protected environments require it. Eligible Linux AMD64/ARM64 and Windows owners can use Depot-managed GitHub runners, while native Depot CI is the candidate for Linux workflow orchestration, matrices, retries, snapshots and test splitting. Under the Developer baseline, Mac work retains GitHub-hosted compute; Startup-trial Mac receipts do not confer Developer eligibility. The demonstrated Linux ARM owners establish selected portability, not every ARM workload. No production trigger or required-check switch follows from this research ([native compatibility](https://depot.dev/docs/ci/compatibility), [runner eligibility](depot-included-allowance-reconciliation.md), [actual ARM consumer](depot-arm64-workload-research.md)).

Allocation preserves three evidence levels: current documentation describes a capability, inspected source establishes its client/schema behavior, and an exact source-bound consumer qualifies only its executed boundary. Native filesystem snapshots, ordinary OCI job/service images, compiled target archives and SDK custom runtimes retain different formats and source/tool identities. The SDK custom thin-image success does not qualify ordinary OCI or named runtimes; planned SDK snapshot and secret APIs are not delivered features ([platform ledger](depot-platform-surface-ledger.json), [reuse controls](depot-reuse-strategy-research.md)).

Native orchestration adoption needs explicit event/check ownership and content-bound artifact names, with selected reusable-workflow references and GitHub-only permissions/environment approvals retained on their supported scheduler. Native retries reuse filesystem/environment state, and native parallel branches share mutable directories; they do not create isolated samples. The completed graph is one job with parallel child branches, not proof of every native parallel-step merge rule. Tests reporting should retain raw JUnit and any validated identity transformation, use attempt-specific report keys, and use historical splitting only for admitted runnable identities. The 34-case Nextest adapter qualifies that shape, while complete-framework reporting, dashboard flakiness and GHA/native analytics parity remain unqualified ([native contracts](depot-native-ci-capability-review.md), [physical adapter](depot-tests-identity-adapter-research.md)).

Debugging and observability are separately scoped capabilities. Native live/paused-step SSH and per-job logs/resource metrics are source-documented; no successful SSH consumer is credited here, and connection strings or signed artifact URLs must remain private. Automatic failed-attempt AI summaries may process masked logs even without an explicit model call; neither stopping diagnose nor disabling CLI tracing opts the organization out. Developer community support, beta terms and the incomplete incident-history denominator provide no repository availability guarantee, so the allocation retains exact-attempt diagnostics and a GitHub execution fallback rather than assuming independent forge availability ([native review](depot-native-ci-capability-review.md), [operating terms and status limits](depot-platform-surface-audit.md#security-and-operational-commitments-under-review)).

draftParagraphs.text: Allocate reuse by actual owner: Gradle remote task outputs for the demonstrated Kotlin linter, direct sccache for the qualified Rust compiler consumers, and source/tool/ABI-bound dependency or target archives where their real readers pass. Do not enable pnpm content-store caching universally on the measured profiles: warm restore plus install did not improve their no-cache boundary. Native tool snapshots are prepared filesystems rather than portable Docker images; they require current checkout and executable/PATH admission. Organization-global Disk mounts need a single writer, partitioning or immutable content; concurrent mounts alone provide no atomicity. Prefer the demonstrated content-bound image and artifact consumers over mutable tag or self-authenticated archive trust ([reuse research](depot-reuse-strategy-research.md), [cache trust review](depot-cache-capability-review.md)).

draftParagraphs.section: Provider allocation, cost, and critical paths
draftParagraphs.text: Use BuildKit/Bake for admitted container contexts and immutable multiarchitecture CI/service producers, preserving the exercised SBOM/provenance-to-runtime-digest checks. A valid subject is not a signature/trust decision. Keep autoscaling off while no total-builder bound is established; its per-instance threshold is not a cap, and minimum per-architecture cache policies are not reserved or hard-limited shared storage. Registry pull-through, Fast CDN and server-side promotion remain source-reviewed options, not measured speedups or activated integrations. Tagged retention is opt-in, saved project images default to unlimited retention, and deletion can precede blob reclamation; Standard transfer is documented free while Fast costs USD 0.10/GB ([BuildKit evidence](../audit/depot-buildkit-platform-campaign-2026-10-18.evidence.json), [registry lifecycle](depot-platform-surface-audit.md#registry-lifecycle-and-export-surface)). Actual credentialed Containerfiles still need their own context and cleanup review: the synthetic Git rewrite control retained its invented-token key, without supplying a real credential or proving exported-layer retention ([source-owned cleanup control](../troubleshooting/git-url-rewrite-cleanup-key.md)).

Before paid scheduling, define a fail-closed admission budget for the controlled jobs and include storage, Tests, SDK and optional products separately. With account-wide billing and usage inspection excluded, an aggregate USD200 invoice guarantee cannot be verified. An owner-issued current monthly headroom/expiry attestation, or explicit paid-admission approval when headroom is unknown, can authorize controlled reservations without granting account access; neither proves unseen charges. Reject unknown or expired admissions and keep the public GitHub compute fallback. Retention and deletion policy must name artifact exports, registry manifests/blobs, snapshots, Disk and logs separately ([allowances and limits](depot-included-allowance-reconciliation.md), [actual logical cleanup](depot-native-buildkit-auth-research.md)).

Treat trust and network exceptions explicitly. Depot Actions caches have the measured cross-branch namespace; project BuildKit caches and organization-global Disk have different boundaries, so untrusted PRs must not inherit trusted cache-write or secret authority by analogy. Linux egress filtering is root-modifiable and incompatible with Tailscale; it is not a hostile-root exfiltration guarantee or a Windows/Mac policy. Static private connectivity requires its documented credentials/tier. Dependabot has a separate runner setting and lacks ordinary GitHub OIDC, so its Depot authentication cannot reuse the regular-job assumption. No such policy, network credential or Dependabot secret was activated ([trust](depot-cache-capability-review.md), [source-reviewed network and bot contracts](depot-platform-surface-ledger.json)).

Keep researched adjacent products explicit rather than silently counting them as adopted: Business Managed/customer-AWS, GPU and custom GHA images require separate eligibility and administrative delegation; native snapshots and ordinary job images do not. Code is a public-beta Git transport/mirror with push-only native events, not a demonstrated independent GitHub recovery path. Depot Agents currently describes Claude Code, Anthropic authentication and separately billed agent minutes without included usage; the repository Codex fixture does not qualify that product. The Dagger engine integration is explicitly deprecated and adds a distinct engine charge, so it is not selected as an expansion route. These source-only integrations remain unactivated, alongside absent-owner cache/language recipes and external observability sinks ([optional-product boundaries](depot-platform-surface-audit.md#agents-code-and-customer-aws-are-distinct-optional-products), [Dagger source](https://depot.dev/docs/github-actions/integrations/dagger)).
